It sets human existence within the sequence of lifelessness, life, death, renewed life, and return to God.
Those fleeing death are still subjected to death and then restored, illustrating that death cannot be escaped.
It states that no soul dies except by God's permission at a written term, directly specifying the limit implicit in 21:34.
Its challenge to avert death if the claimants are truthful makes death's inevitability an explicit test.
It declares that death will reach people wherever they are, giving a concise universal counterpart to the focus ayah.
It names both a human term and an appointed term with God, reinforcing mortality as a fixed divine limit.
It joins human life, death, and eventual emergence, supplying the full temporal arc absent from claims of immortality.
It states that every community has an appointed term which cannot be delayed or advanced.
It repeats the fixed term of each community, directly supporting the denial of indefinite continuance.
It says that once the appointed term arrives it cannot be postponed or brought forward, closely defining mortal finitude.
It traces human creation, death, and declining old age, contrasting human dependence with any claim to permanence.
It presents humans as from the earth, returned to it, and brought out again, linking death to resurrection.
Its stages of human development, old age, death, and resurrection make mortality part of created human existence.
It explicitly says God gives life, then causes death, then gives life again.
Its direct address says that humans will surely die after their present life.
It immediately completes the death statement with resurrection on the Day of Rising.
It denies that alleged gods possess death, life, or resurrection, clarifying whose power frames human mortality.
It describes all prior messengers as eating food and walking in markets, supporting their ordinary human condition.
It contrasts the Messenger's mortal condition with the Ever-Living One who never dies.
It declares that everything perishes except God, supplying a decisive contrast to any created being's immortality.
It repeats that every soul tastes death and adds the return to God, complementing the immediate context in 21:35.
It gives the sequence of creation, provision, death, and renewed life as God's action upon humanity.
It says no soul knows in what land it will die, emphasizing the creature's lack of control over death.
It identifies the angel of death's taking of souls before their return to God.
It denies that fleeing can benefit anyone fleeing death or killing.
It contrasts humanity's neediness with God's self-sufficiency, a theological boundary behind the denial of human permanence.
It recalls how many generations before the audience were destroyed and do not return to worldly life.
It shows that even a long-lived human is reversed in creation, directly undermining permanence inferred from longevity.
It directly tells the Messenger that he will die and tells his opponents that they too will die.
It describes God taking souls at death and during sleep, locating life and death under divine possession.
It traces human creation through maturity and old age to a specified term, explicitly denying autonomous continuance.
It states that God gives life and causes death, grounding the focus ayah in divine agency.
It identifies God as the one who gives life and causes death, contrasting divine agency with human mortality.
It names the inescapable agony of death as the event people try to avoid.
It declares that God gives life and causes death and that all return to Him.
It concisely attributes both death and life to God.
It declares that everyone upon the earth will perish, a broad direct parallel to 21:34's denial of immortality.
It immediately contrasts universal perishing with the enduring Lord.
It says death has been apportioned among humanity and cannot be outstripped.
Its image of the soul reaching the throat confronts the human inability to prevent death.
It attributes dominion, life, and death to God, supplying the sovereign frame for the focus claim.
It says the death people flee will surely meet them before their return to the Knower of the unseen and seen.
It states that God does not defer a soul when its appointed term has come.
It names death and life as created realities, directly framing mortality as deliberate divine creation.
It begins the immediate description of death as the soul reaches the collarbone.
It places human death and burial before later resurrection, completing the created human cycle.
